A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoEval Done Right and provide readable text, equations, figures, and code snippets. The complete documents were inspected: v1 has no appendix, while v2 includes Supplements A and B.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet model-evaluation experiments and LLM preference analyses, including accuracy, confidence intervals, effective sample sizes, and rankings.

after.justification: v2 retains original ImageNet and LLM evaluations and adds protein-fitness experiments, annotator-quality analysis, and supplementary results.

M1.justification: The general metric estimator, synthetic-label weighting, and Bradley–Terry fitting procedure are retained. Protein correlation estimation specializes the existing framework using an external annotator, which v1 already permits. The argmax-to-argmin equation correction matches the minimization procedure already described in v1.

E1.justification: Section 2.4 adds protein-fitness regression evaluation on the ProteinGym protein G assay, containing 536,962 pairwise mutations, substantially extending coverage beyond ImageNet classification and LLM preferences. The LLM win-rate task already appears in v1 Figure 1; its supplementary expansion is not a new task.

E2.justification: The synthetic-label-only imputation comparator, called naive in v1 Figure 3, disappears from the corresponding LLM evaluation in v2. PPI, PPI++, and classical estimation remain. The new protein experiment uses this retained estimator comparison set.

E3.justification: The Bradley–Terry evaluation expands from the n = 25 example in v1 to budgets of 50–150 labeled observations with MSE, ESS, ranking, and interval diagnostics. Protein evaluation introduces standardized Pearson correlation and held-out VESPA predictions. Section 2.3 also corrects the reported fixed PPI weight from lambda = 0 to 1; this does not establish how the earlier implementation ran.

E4.justification: New Figure 4 tests how eight protein annotators of differing quality affect PPI++ effective sample size at n = 500. Supplement B.1 adds confidence-interval calibration and width analyses for protein correlations and Bradley–Terry coefficients. ImageNet interval diagnostics already existed in v1 Figure 2 and are retained in reorganized form.

E5.justification: v1 specifies 500 random splits for ImageNet; v2 specifies 250 splits throughout, newly documenting repetition counts for the LLM analyses. The asymptotic confidence-interval framework and Bonferroni ranking correction remain. The reported count change should not be interpreted as an increase in replication.

E6.justification: v2 replaces the n = 25 model-specific Bradley–Terry results with aggregate curves reporting a 20–25% ESS advantage for PPI++. New protein results report approximately 50% higher ESS and show unoptimized PPI underperforming classical estimation. Figure S2 adds win-rate MSE results, and Table 1 adds execution times. These are added or revised evaluations, not same-setting performance gains over v1.

T1.justification: The Bradley–Terry estimator changes from argmax in v1 Equation 18 to argmin in v2 Equation 15, correcting its inconsistency with the stated loss-minimization argument. The general bias, variance, and confidence-set mathematics remains, without new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract is unchanged, retaining claims of unbiased, more sample-efficient autoevaluation and up to 50% effective human-labeled sample-size improvement with gpt-4. The contribution remains a practical PPI instantiation for metric and pairwise evaluation, including synthetic label distributions. Protein experiments support this existing generality claim.

C2.justification: The protein discussion adds interpretation of unoptimized PPI's failure and the usefulness of PPI++ with mediocre annotators. The previous explanation that naive LLM evaluation exaggerates performance differences is removed with that comparison. The requirement for representative data and the distribution-shift limitation remain.

D1.justification: Supplement A adds the protein assay identifier and normalization, averaging of repeated human annotations, hardware specifications, JAX implementation details for Bradley–Terry experiments, and execution times. These are newly documented details, not established implementation changes. Conversely, v2 removes the dedicated experimental-code repository link while retaining the ppi_py link and identical code snippets.

R1.justification: Related Work adds BLEU, ROUGE, automatic-metric statistical advantages, and Chaganty et al.'s control-variate debiasing work. Protein-modeling and JAX references are added, while the ImageNet dataset and Elo references are removed. The central positioning relative to PPI, AIPW, and concurrent autoevaluation research remains.

P1.justification: Most introductory and methodological prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 revises experimental summaries, consolidates ImageNet result paragraphs, adds explicit Limitations and Broader Impacts headings, and introduces supplementary sections. Author affiliations and contact information are added, while the acknowledgements and standalone availability section are removed.

P2.justification: ImageNet Figure 2 changes from six panels to three, with interval diagnostics moved to Figure S1 and the individual accuracy-interval illustration removed. The old model-specific LLM plot is replaced by aggregate curves. Protein, annotator-quality, and supplementary win-rate plots and a runtime table are added, alongside extensive figure restyling and document reformatting.

improvement.justification: The protein regression and annotator-quality studies address important gaps in v1's empirical support for general metric evaluation and weak synthetic labels. The expanded Bradley–Terry evaluation assesses error, ranking, and calibration across sample budgets instead of relying on one interval example. Supplement A and the optimization correction improve reproducibility and mathematical clarity. These substantial gains outweigh the loss of the naive comparator and direct experimental-code link.
